title: What Does Fréchet Distance Measure? A Directional Decomposition

paper.title: What Does Fréchet Distance Measure? A Directional Decomposition
paper.abstract:
Abstract The Fréchet distance is a de facto standard for evaluating generative models across domains, appearing as FID for images and FVD for videos. It summarizes the discrepancy between generated and reference distributions in a single scalar, with lower values typically interpreted as better generation quality. However, this scalar view can obscure what drives the comparison. For example, in COCO dataset, increasing the number of diffusion sampling steps improves ImageReward scores yet worsens (increases) FID. Motivated by this mismatch, we seek to make the Fréchet distance more interpretable by uncovering where the discrepancy lies. To this end, we introduce directional Fréchet distance , the expected squared projection of the optimal transport displacement onto a given direction.
Across our image, video, and protein case studies, we find that a small number of interpretable directions account for much of the distance. We use these directions to explain the FID increase in terms of semantic concepts represented by CLIP embeddings, quantify FVD’s bias toward per-frame appearance, and revisit the interpretation of Protein FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/yhlee-add/directional-fd .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Fréchet distance ( Dowson and Landau, 1982 ) underlies de facto evaluation metrics for generative models in continuous domains: Fréchet Inception distance (FID) for images ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , Fréchet video distance (FVD) for videos ( Unterthiner et al., 2018 ) , and Fréchet audio distance (FAD) for audio ( Kilgour et al., 2018 ) . A lower distance is read as a better generator, so the metric does not merely report progress but also defines it , steering architecture, sampling, and hyperparameter choices ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) . This influential signal, however, remains a scalar summary of a comparison between two high-dimensional feature distributions. This blind spot surfaces in recurring contradictions. For images, tuning a diffusion sampler configuration to minimize FID can drive per-sample quality to its worst ( Lee et al., 2026 ) ; stronger image distortions can even improve (lower) the metric ( Jayasumana et al., 2024 ) ; additional sampling steps can produce visibly sharper images ( Choi et al., 2025 ) , yet worsen FID on the COCO dataset ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . For videos, FVD favors per-frame appearance over motion, so a flickering clip can still score well ( Ge et al., 2024 ) . Prior work has sought to address these issues by refining Fréchet metrics or introducing scalar alternatives , such as changing the embedding ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2022 ) , adopting a kernel two-sample statistic ( Bińkowski et al., 2018 ; Jayasumana et al., 2024 ) , or reducing estimator bias ( Chong and Forsyth, 2020 ) . These changes can mitigate specific failures, but the resulting metrics still do not reveal where in feature space the distributions differ or what the discrepancy means. Contribution. In this work, we take a complementary approach: making existing Fréchet metrics interpretable. We introduce directional Fréchet distance , which measures the contribution of a fixed feature direction to the Fréchet distance. These directional distances sum to the Fréchet distance over any orthonormal basis, and the top eigenvectors of the displacement second-moment matrix inform where the discrepancy concentrates. We further affix these directions to interpretable concepts using CLIP concept bridges ( Kim et al., 2018 ; Bhalla et al., 2024 ) for images and structural-property concept directions for proteins. This gives semantic meaning to directional distances : a larger distance along a direction associated with a concept, e.g., composition simplicity or brightness, indicates that the metric attributes more of the discrepancy between generated and reference samples to that concept. With this lens, we revisit three established Fréchet metrics—FID, FVD, and Protein FID—to explain what drives previously reported discrepancies: • Images: In some reference datasets such as COCO, additional sampling steps can increase ImageReward but also increase FID ( Lee and Pak, 2026 ) . We find that two-thirds of this increase lies along a single direction in the feature space associated with composition simplicity. • Videos: In the controlled distortions of Ge et al. (2024) , I3D-based FVD responds weakly to added flicker. We find that the flicker band carries less of the distance than the appearance band with I3D features, but more with VideoMAE-v2 features. • Proteins: Protein FID was introduced to detect collapse onto a narrow range of easily foldable structures ( Faltings et al., 2025 ) , and its observed gap was partly attributed to missing beta sheets. We find that a single direction associated with structural regularity accounts for most of the gap, while the alpha-versus-beta direction accounts for little.

sections.heading: 2 Preliminaries
sections.text: In Section 2.1 , we review the Fréchet distance and the family of metrics built from it. In Section 2.2 , we revisit prior observations across images and videos whose apparent contradictions stem from reading this single number as a measure of per-sample quality.

sections.heading: 2.1 The Fréchet distance and its instances
sections.text: Fréchet distance is widely used to evaluate generative models by comparing Gaussian approximations to generated and reference distributions in a fixed feature space. A prominent example is Fréchet Inception distance (FID) ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , which uses InceptionV3 ( Szegedy et al., 2016 ) features. The Fréchet distance is the squared 2-Wasserstein distance between the fitted Gaussians, which admits the closed form FD = ‖ μ r − μ g ‖ 2 + Tr ⁡ ( Σ r + Σ g − 2 ​ ( Σ r 1 / 2 ​ Σ g ​ Σ r 1 / 2 ) 1 / 2 ) , \mathrm{FD}=\|\mu_{r}-\mu_{g}\|^{2}+\Tr\left(\Sigma_{r}+\Sigma_{g}-2\left(\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}\Sigma_{g}\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}\right)^{1/2}\right), (1) where ( μ r , Σ r ) (\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r}) and ( μ g , Σ g ) (\mu_{g},\Sigma_{g}) are the mean and covariance of the reference and generated feature distributions. The same Fréchet distance can also be computed over other embeddings such as CLIP ViT-L/14 ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) . The same recipe extends the metric across domains: Video is evaluated with FVD ( Unterthiner et al., 2018 ) , the Fréchet distance over I3D embeddings ( Carreira and Zisserman, 2017 ) , and protein structure generation has recently adopted Protein FID ( Faltings et al., 2025 ) over ESM3 structure-token embeddings ( Hayes et al., 2025 ) . Across all of these, a full comparison between two distributions is reduced to a single number, which reports that they differ but not where .

sections.heading: 2.2 Contradictory observations
sections.text: A lower Fréchet distance is commonly interpreted as a higher-quality generator. This interpretation suggests that improvements in per-sample quality should be accompanied by a decrease in distance. In this section, we present two prior observations that challenge this. To begin with, we first formally define the per-sample quality : for a chosen sample-level scoring function q q , we denote the quality of generator G G to be 𝔼 x ∼ G ​ [ q ​ ( x ) ] \mathbb{E}_{x\sim G}[q(x)] . Examples of such scoring functions include CLIP score ( Hessel et al., 2021 ) , ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , and the numerical accuracy of each sample. Figure 1: Sign reversal on SD1.5/COCO under two standard knobs. As the classifier-free guidance scale (left) or the number of sampling steps (right) increases, per-sample quality rises while FID worsens. A lower FID therefore does not track higher per-sample quality. Images. Two standard knobs on Stable Diffusion 1.5 (SD1.5, Rombach et al., 2022 ) make this concrete (Figure 1 ). Raising the classifier-free guidance scale ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) makes each sample match the prompt better and improves ImageReward, yet FID on the COCO reference dataset ( Lin et al., 2014 ) worsens monotonically ( Lee et al., 2026 , Table 8) . Using more denoising steps reduces numerical error in each sample and also improves ImageReward ( Lee and Pak, 2026 ) , but FID can rise ( Choi et al., 2025 , Table 1) or converge ( Lu et al., 2025 , Section 7.2) . We call this contradictory phenomenon sign reversal : a change that raises per-sample quality raises the Fréchet distance instead of lowering it. Sign reversal makes FID an unreliable gate on generation quality. A sampling algorithm ( Lu et al., 2025 ) or an inference accelerator ( Kim et al., 2025 ) is accepted once it matches or lowers FID, read as evidence that quality is preserved. Under sign reversal, that inference is invalid, since the same low FID is equally consistent with per-sample quality having dropped, and the verdict on the method no longer follows. Videos. FVD computes the Fréchet distance in the feature space of I3D ( Carreira and Zisserman, 2017 ) , a video model pretrained for action recognition. In practice, however, FVD favors per-frame appearance over motion ( Ge et al., 2024 ) : a clip whose individual frames are realistic can still score well when it flickers. To address this, Ge et al. (2024) propose replacing I3D features with self-supervised video embeddings such as VideoMAE-v2 ( Wang et al., 2023b ) , improving sensitivity to motion while retaining the same Fréchet distance computation.

sections.heading: 3 Directional Fréchet distance
sections.text: The contradictory observations of Section 2.2 highlight a limitation of interpreting Fréchet distance (FD) as a measure of per-sample quality: FD aggregates discrepancies across feature directions into a single value, obscuring which of them drive it. We therefore introduce directional Fréchet distance , the contribution of a given direction to FD, which recovers directional information that is encoded in the means and covariances used to compute FD but lost in the final number. Directional Fréchet distance. To define directional Fréchet distance, we first express FD as an optimal transport cost. Assuming that two Gaussian distributions 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ r , Σ r ) \mathcal{N}(\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r}) and 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ g , Σ g ) \mathcal{N}(\mu_{g},\Sigma_{g}) , which are defined by the first and second moments of the reference and generated distributions, are both nondegenerate, the FD in equation 1 is defined by ( Knott and Smith, 1984 ; Peyré and Cuturi, 2019 ) FD = 𝔼 [ ‖ x − T ( x ) ‖ 2 ] , T ( x ) := μ g + A ( x − μ r ) , A = Σ r − 1 / 2 ( Σ r 1 / 2 Σ g Σ r 1 / 2 ) 1 / 2 Σ r − 1 / 2 . \mathrm{FD}=\mathbb{E}[\left\|x-T(x)\right\|^{2}],\quad T(x):=\mu_{g}+A(x-\mu_{r}),\quad A=\Sigma_{r}^{-1/2}\left(\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}\Sigma_{g}\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}\right)^{1/2}\Sigma_{r}^{-1/2}. The expectation is calculated over x ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ r , Σ r ) x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r}) . Here, one can show that T T is the optimal transport map between 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ r , Σ r ) \mathcal{N}(\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r}) and 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ g , Σ g ) \mathcal{N}(\mu_{g},\Sigma_{g}) , i.e., it minimizes the expected squared norm among all measurable maps that transport 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ r , Σ r ) \mathcal{N}(\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r}) to 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ g , Σ g ) \mathcal{N}(\mu_{g},\Sigma_{g}) : T = argmin S ​ 𝔼 x ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ r , Σ r ) ​ [ ‖ x − S ⁡ ( x ) ‖ 2 ] , T=\mathrm{argmin}_{S}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r})}[\left\|x-S(x)\right\|^{2}], where the argmin is taken over all maps S S satisfying S ⁡ ( x ) ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ g , Σ g ) S(x)\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{g},\Sigma_{g}) when x ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ r , Σ r ) x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r}) . Now we define directional Fréchet distance . For a given unit direction w w , the directional Fréchet distance FD ⁡ ( w ) \mathrm{FD}(w) is computed as the squared distance along w w under the optimal transport map T T , i.e., FD ⁡ ( w ) := 𝔼 x ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ r , Σ r ) ​ [ ( w ⊤ ​ ( x − T ⁡ ( x ) ) ) 2 ] . \mathrm{FD}(w):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r})}[(w^{\top}(x-T(x)))^{2}]. An alternative way to formulate FD ⁡ ( w ) \mathrm{FD}(w) is to introduce the displacement second-moment matrix ( Paty and Cuturi, 2019 ; Meng et al., 2020 ) M = 𝔼 x ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ r , Σ r ) ​ [ ( x − T ⁡ ( x ) ) ​ ( x − T ⁡ ( x ) ) ⊤ ] M=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r})}\left[(x-T(x))(x-T(x))^{\top}\right] , resulting in FD ⁡ ( w ) = w ⊤ ​ M ​ w \mathrm{FD}(w)=w^{\top}Mw . Therefore, for any orthonormal basis { w k } \{w_{k}\} , directional Fréchet distances sum to the Fréchet distance, FD = ∑ k FD ⁡ ( w k ) \mathrm{FD}=\sum_{k}\mathrm{FD}(w_{k}) (Appendix B ). Interpretation. A large FD ⁡ ( w ) \mathrm{FD}(w) indicates that displacement along w w contributes substantially to the optimal transport cost between the generated and reference Gaussians. This decomposition thus provides a diagnostic tool for understanding what drives FD. For instance, when a direction is associated with an interpretable concept, such as brightness or composition simplicity, its directional FD quantifies how much of the discrepancy between the generated and reference distributions is attributed to that concept direction.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we use directional Fréchet distance to revisit three Fréchet metrics. We first explain why additional denoising steps raise ImageReward but also raise FID, and why the sign of this effect flips across references (Section 4.1 ). We then explain why VideoMAE-v2 makes FVD more sensitive to flicker than I3D (Section 4.2 ). Finally, we examine which structural directions drive the Protein FID gap ( Faltings et al., 2025 ) (Section 4.3 ). Each case study follows a common procedure. We take the top eigenvectors e 1 , e 2 , … e_{1},e_{2},\dots of a displacement second-moment matrix M M (Section 3 ), which identify the directions along which a distance concentrates. We then interpret these directions within each domain (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: 4.1 Sign reversal
sections.text: We study sign reversal on images in the common setting of FID on the COCO reference, where additional denoising steps on Stable Diffusion 1.5 (SD1.5) raise ImageReward score but also raise FID (Figure 1 ). We build the explanation in two steps: (1) what the top directions mean, (2) then which of them carries the change in FID and why its sign flips across references. We first analyze a single comparison, SD1.5 at 50 50 steps against COCO, to find the directions FID concentrates on and name them with concept dictionaries (Section 4.1.1 ). We then sweep the denoising steps and follow which of these directions carries the change in FID, first on COCO and then across six references, to explain what sets its sign (Section 4.1.2 ).

sections.heading: 4.1.1 Naming the top directions
sections.text: We evaluate SD1.5 at 50 50 denoising steps against the COCO reference in Inception feature space, where FID is 14.6 14.6 , and ask three questions of this single comparison: where in feature space the distance concentrates, what those directions mean, and how the two distributions differ along them. Where: FID concentrates on a few directions. Ordering the eigenvectors e 1 , e 2 , … e_{1},e_{2},\dots of M M by their directional FD ranks the feature directions by the share of FID they carry, and the spectrum is steep: e 1 e_{1} carries 24.0 % 24.0\% of FID, e 2 e_{2} carries 3.8 % 3.8\% , and e 3 e_{3} carries 2.5 % 2.5\% , so three eigenvectors account for 30.3 % 30.3\% of a distance computed across 2048 2048 feature dimensions. What: CLIP as a bridge. A substantial fraction of FID thus concentrates on three directions, but these are directions in Inception feature space and have no semantics on their own, so naming them is what turns the decomposition into a statement about how the reference and generated sets differ. We attach meaning with CLIP as a bridge between text and the Inception features FID is computed in. We write a CLIP dictionary of 24 24 photographic concepts, each a pair of opposing prompt sets, e.g. a single clean subject against a cluttered scene, and embed both poles with the CLIP text encoder. sections.heading: 4.1.2 Which directions carry the reversal
sections.text: We next use this decomposition to identify which directions account for sign reversal. Using SD1.5 and COCO again, we take eight generated sets using { 15 , 20 , … , 50 } \{15,20,\dots,50\} steps. To track the same directions across these settings, we fix the eigenbasis of the 50 50 -step M M and regress each direction’s FD ⁡ ( e i ) \mathrm{FD}(e_{i}) against the total FID; since the directional FDs over the basis sum to FD, the slopes sum to one, and each slope is the fraction of the FD change the direction carries (Figure 3 ). One eigenvector accounts for two thirds of the increase. The top eigenvector e 1 e_{1} has slope 0.66 0.66 ( R 2 = 0.96 R^{2}=0.96 ), while e 2 e_{2} and e 3 e_{3} stay nearly flat at slopes 0.03 0.03 and 0.02 0.02 , so two thirds of the FID increase lives on e 1 e_{1} alone. FID thus rises with steps mainly because the generated mean drifts further toward simpler, single-object images and away from COCO, which ties most of the sign reversal of Section 2.2 to one named direction (Appendix D ). Since the directional FDs of all D D eigenvectors sum to FID, s 1 : D = 1 s_{1:D}=1 . The curve rises above one, peaking at 1.62 1.62 near i = 440 i=440 , and then falls back to one; we call the eigenvectors up to this peak the head and the rest the tail . sections.heading: 4.2 Video content bias
sections.text: Fréchet video distance (FVD, Unterthiner et al., 2018 ) is the Fréchet distance over the features of I3D ( Carreira and Zisserman, 2017 ) , which is an action-recognition model. Ge et al. (2024) expose the content bias of FVD (Section 2.2 ) by decoupling per-frame appearance from motion. In particular, they create two sets of degraded real videos: one with the same distortion across frames and another with a distortion of matched severity resampled each frame. They find that I3D-based FVD barely penalizes the resulting flicker. To address this bias, they replace I3D with VideoMAE-v2 ( Wang et al., 2023b ) , which makes FVD more sensitive to flicker. We use directional FD to explain this difference: in I3D feature space, appearance-related directions account for more of the spatio-temporally distorted set’s distance from real videos than flicker-related directions, whereas in VideoMAE-v2 feature space, the ordering reverses. Decoupled distortions as probes. We obtain these directions from the two degraded sets of Ge et al. (2024) , which we rebuild on a reference set R R of 2048 2048 UCF-101 clips of 16 16 frames ( Soomro et al., 2012 ) . The distortions are elastic transformation and motion blur, each at the five severities of ImageNet-C ( Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019 ) . The appearance set S S is their spatially distorted set, which applies one sampled distortion to every frame of a clip. The flicker set T T is their spatio-temporally distorted set, which resamples the distortion at every frame. The two sets share the distribution of per-frame distortions, so T T differs from S S only by the flicker. Appearance and flicker displacements. We write M ⁡ ( P , Q ) M(P,Q) for the displacement second-moment matrix between two sets P P and Q Q . The appearance displacement M ⁡ ( R , S ) M(R,S) reflects the distortion itself. The flicker displacement M ⁡ ( S , T ) M(S,T) reflects the flicker added on top of it. We average each displacement over severities and take its top eigenvectors as the appearance band and the flicker band . The cumulative share ∑ i ≤ k FD ⁡ ( e i ) / FD \sum_{i\leq k}\mathrm{FD}(e_{i})/\mathrm{FD} is the fraction of a set’s FD that the top k k eigenvectors e i e_{i} of a band carry. The two bands are computed independently and can overlap. A share therefore measures how much of a distance aligns with a band, not an exclusive allocation between the bands (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: 4.2.2 A real generator on the bands
sections.text: The bands so far come from controlled distortions. We now ask whether the content bias found on the flicker set (Section 4.2.1 ) also appears in a real generator’s discrepancy from the reference. We sample a set G G of 2048 2048 clips with ModelScope text-to-video ( Wang et al., 2023a ) , zero-shot on the UCF-101 class names. We then evaluate its displacement M ⁡ ( R , G ) M(R,G) on the appearance and flicker bands under both embeddings. VideoMAE shifts the generated distance toward the flicker band. I3D puts about twice as much of M ⁡ ( R , G ) M(R,G) on the appearance band as on the flicker band, with 0.29 0.29 against 0.15 0.15 on the motion blur bands at k = 10 k=10 (Table 2 ). This is the same ordering as on the flicker set. VideoMAE splits the same distance evenly, with 0.095 0.095 against 0.096 0.096 . The ratio of the flicker share to the appearance share thus rises from 0.52 0.52 under I3D to 1.01 1.01 under VideoMAE. The elastic bands show the same shift, from 0.37 0.37 to 0.57 0.57 , although appearance still leads there (Appendix F ). Finding. VideoMAE shifts a real generator’s distance toward the flicker band. The two motion blur bands carry it evenly under VideoMAE, while I3D puts twice as much on the appearance band. A scalar ratio cannot report this shift upon an arbitrary generated set.

sections.heading: 4.3 Protein FID attribution
sections.text: Designability is the most widely used per-sample metric for protein backbones: An inverse-folding model designs a sequence for the backbone, which is then refolded by a structure predictor. The backbone is considered designable if the predicted structure matches it within a self-consistency RMSD (scRMSD) of 2 2 Å ( Trippe et al., 2022 ; Watson et al., 2023 ) . High designability, however, can be achieved by generating mostly alpha-helical backbones: alpha helices rely largely on local hydrogen bonds, whereas beta sheets require long-range coordination. Optimizing for designability can therefore favor a narrow range of easily foldable, helix-rich structures while losing beta sheets from the generated distribution. To detect such collapse, Faltings et al. (2025) introduce Protein FID, the Fréchet distance between generated and reference structures embedded with the ESM3 structure encoder ( Hayes et al., 2025 ) . They validate it through its monotone response to structural perturbations and its recovery of the FoldSeek and CATH hierarchies. The authors partly attribute the Protein FID gap to missing beta sheets, based on a sample-level influence analysis that identifies large alpha-helical bundles as major contributors. We use directional FD to examine which structural directions drive the gap: the alpha-versus-beta contrast accounts for only a small share, whereas a single direction associated with structural regularity accounts for the largest share. Reference and embedding. Protein FID mean-pools the per-residue ESM3 embeddings to 1536 1536 dimensions. It then applies a PCA to 32 32 dimensions, fit jointly over the reference and generated embeddings, because the raw covariances are nearly degenerate ( Faltings et al., 2025 ) . We analyze this 32 32 -dimensional space and recompute the optimal transport in it. The reference is the released embeddings of curated PDB structures. The raw space gives the same picture (Appendix G ). Generations and concept directions. We generate unconditional backbones with La-Proteina ( Geffner et al., 2026 ) , 467 467 structures per setting, following the Protein FID protocol. To interpret the eigenvectors of M M , we build a concept dictionary in the same space. We define the alpha-versus-beta direction using the mainly-alpha and mainly-beta CATH classes ( Sillitoe et al., 2021 ) , and additional concepts by splitting ten whole-structure geometric properties into terciles. Each concept direction is a difference between group means of CATH embeddings, projected onto the same PCA basis. We then fit each eigenvector with a Lasso over this dictionary, as in Section 4.1.1 .

sections.text: We analyze La-Proteina at 400 400 steps against the reference and ask the three questions of Section 4.1.1 : where, what, and how. Where: the distance concentrates on one direction. The spectrum of M M is steep: e 1 e_{1} carries 66 % 66\% of Protein FID, e 2 e_{2} carries 14 % 14\% , and e 3 e_{3} carries 4 % 4\% . sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduced directional Fréchet distance, decomposing Fréchet distance along an orthonormal basis of feature directions. Across images, videos, and proteins, this viewpoint facilitates explaining the sign reversal of FID and the content bias of FVD, and revisits a prior interpretation of Protein FID. Outlook. More broadly, we hope this work prompts a rethinking of what scalar evaluation can and cannot tell us. A scalar score is useful per se –it makes models easy to compare, spurring competition and progress in generative modeling. Nevertheless, it does not reveal which aspects of a distribution a model fails to capture. Directional FD opens the door to more interpretable evaluation of generative models.

sections.heading: Critiques of FID.
sections.text: A line of work critiques the estimator and the space it lives in. Inception embeddings of standard datasets fail multivariate normality tests, violating the Gaussian assumption ( Jayasumana et al., 2024 ) . FID is a biased estimator whose bias depends on the model being evaluated, not just on the sample count ( Chong and Forsyth, 2020 ) . Differences in image resizing also shift it by several points on identical data ( Parmar et al., 2022 ) . The representation matters as much as the estimator. The second-last layer of InceptionV3 is one affine transform from the ImageNet logits, so FID is sensitive to ImageNet class information that need not reflect perceptual quality ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2022 ) . The semantics an embedding encodes also depend strongly on its training ( Stein et al., 2023 ) . Surveys of evaluation practice add that the choice of metric is rarely motivated and that automatic metrics often disagree with human judgment ( Borji, 2022 ; Otani et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Swapping one scalar metric for another.
sections.text: Each pathology has typically been mitigated by replacing one scalar metric with another. Examples include a cleaner embedding ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2022 ) , a different kernel such as the MMD tests of KID ( Bińkowski et al., 2018 ) and CMMD ( Jayasumana et al., 2024 ) , a debiased estimator ( Chong and Forsyth, 2020 ) , and a content-debiased FVD that traces the video bias to the embedding ( Ge et al., 2024 ) . Protein FID ( Faltings et al., 2025 ) is the same move in a new domain, swapping the per-sample designability score for a distributional metric. These works support their diagnoses with further analyses. The metric each proposes, however, still reports a single number, which does not show where in feature space the discrepancy lives.

sections.heading: Reporting more than one number.
sections.text: The closest attempts to report more than one number measure a generator along two fixed criteria. Precision and recall separate sample fidelity from distributional coverage ( Sajjadi et al., 2018 ; Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019 ) , and density and coverage make those two criteria more robust to outliers ( Naeem et al., 2020 ) . These measures are informative but preset. They score a generator on fidelity and diversity, not along data-driven or semantically named directions.

sections.heading: The displacement second-moment matrix.
sections.text: The matrix M M whose directions we name is not new to optimal transport. Paty and Cuturi (2019) define the second moment V π = ∫ ( x − y ) ​ ( x − y ) ⊤ ​ 𝑑 π ​ ( x , y ) V_{\pi}=\int(x-y)(x-y)^{\top}d\pi(x,y) of the displacements under a coupling π \pi and note that its trace is the transport cost. They build subspace-robust Wasserstein distances from its top eigenvalues, optimizing the coupling and the subspace jointly. Meng et al. (2020) use the eigenvectors of the same second moment as a supervised projection for dimension reduction. Both use the matrix to define a new distance or a new projection. We instead keep the coupling fixed at the Gaussian optimal map behind an existing metric. sections.heading: Interpreting feature directions.
sections.text: A separate literature interprets the directions of a feature space rather than the metric. Concept activation vectors probe a representation along human-named concept directions ( Kim et al., 2018 ) , SpLiCE decomposes CLIP embeddings into a sparse sum of interpretable concepts ( Bhalla et al., 2024 ) , and sparse autoencoders recover interpretable features from protein language models ( Simon and Zou, 2025 ) . We reuse this machinery, but to name the directions a Fréchet metric charges for rather than to interpret an embedding in isolation.

The mean part of M M has rank one, so a dominant mean gap draws the top eigenvector e 1 e_{1} toward the mean-difference direction δ / ‖ δ ‖ \delta/\|\delta\| . The covariance part then decides the eigenvectors that follow.

sections.heading: Directional FD is not the FD of a projection.
sections.text: The pair ( w ⊤ ​ x , w ⊤ ​ T ​ ( x ) ) (w^{\top}x,w^{\top}T(x)) with x ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ r , Σ r ) x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r}) is one coupling of the two projected Gaussians. Its cost FD ⁡ ( w ) \mathrm{FD}(w) is therefore at least their optimal cost, the Fréchet distance ( w ⊤ ​ δ ) 2 + ( w ⊤ ​ Σ r ​ w − w ⊤ ​ Σ g ​ w ) 2 (w^{\top}\delta)^{2}+(\sqrt{w^{\top}\Sigma_{r}w}-\sqrt{w^{\top}\Sigma_{g}w})^{2} between the projections. The inequality can be strict, because the optimal coupling of the full distributions need not couple the projections optimally. For example, two covariances may differ only in how their coordinates correlate. Their projections onto each coordinate then coincide, but the map still pays along every coordinate to rotate the correlation. The projected means and variances, which we report as Cohen’s d d and the variance ratio, thus describe how the two sets differ along w w . The same bound holds for a subspace. The directional FD of a subspace with orthogonal projector P P is Tr ⁡ ( P ​ M ) \Tr(PM) , the sum of FD ⁡ ( w ) \mathrm{FD}(w) over an orthonormal basis of the subspace. Protein FID is the Fréchet distance between the projections onto a 32 32 -dimensional PCA subspace. It is therefore not the directional FD of that subspace in the raw space, but a lower bound on it.

sections.text: Section 3 assumes both Gaussians nondegenerate, but the map needs only a nondegenerate Σ r \Sigma_{r} . This covers the raw 1536 1536 -dimensional protein analysis of Appendix G . sections.heading: Numerical computation.
sections.text: We compute in float64 and take every matrix square root from an eigendecomposition, which is real for any positive semidefinite input. Most implementations of FD instead apply scipy.linalg.sqrtm , a Schur decomposition, to the non-symmetric product of the two covariances. This returns spurious imaginary parts when the product is singular, although the true square root is real. The reference implementation of Protein FID ( Faltings et al., 2025 ) is one of them and rejects the result once the imaginary part exceeds a fixed tolerance. It therefore fails on a generated set of 32 32 structures, whose covariance is singular in the 32 32 -dimensional PCA space, and succeeds on 40 40 . Directional FD also needs the inverse square root in A A . We avoid it by assembling the covariance part of M M as Σ r + Σ g − K − K ⊤ \Sigma_{r}+\Sigma_{g}-K-K^{\top} , where K = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( x − μ r ) ​ ( T ⁡ ( x ) − μ g ) ⊤ ] = Σ r ​ A K=\mathbb{E}[(x-\mu_{r})(T(x)-\mu_{g})^{\top}]=\Sigma_{r}A is the cross-covariance under the optimal coupling. We obtain K = Σ r 1 / 2 ​ W ⊤ ​ Σ g 1 / 2 K=\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}W^{\top}\Sigma_{g}^{1/2} from the polar decomposition Σ g 1 / 2 ​ Σ r 1 / 2 = W ​ P \Sigma_{g}^{1/2}\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}=WP into an orthogonal W W and a positive semidefinite P P . This polar decomposition requires no inversion and exists for singular covariances too.

sections.text: Each eigenvector e i e_{i} of M M is oriented toward the generated mean, e i ⊤ ​ ( μ g − μ r ) ≥ 0 e_{i}^{\top}(\mu_{g}-\mu_{r})\geq 0 , so + e i +e_{i} is the generated end. Cohen’s d d along a direction is the difference between the means of the generated and reference projections, divided by their pooled standard deviation. The variance ratio is the variance of the generated projections over that of the reference projections. A concept direction w c w_{c} is the unit-normalized difference between the mean features of two groups of real samples, computed in the space that defines the metric. The groups are reference images ranked by CLIP image-text similarity for images, and CATH domains split by class or by a geometric property for proteins. The sparse concept fit regresses e i e_{i} on the concept directions of one dictionary with a Lasso without intercept, min β ⁡ 1 2 ​ D ​ ‖ e i − W ​ β ‖ 2 + α ​ ‖ β ‖ 1 \min_{\beta}\frac{1}{2D}\|e_{i}-W\beta\|^{2}+\alpha\|\beta\|_{1} , where the columns of W W are the concept directions in D D dimensions. It reports the surviving signed weights and the cosine between e i e_{i} and its reconstruction W ​ β W\beta . A weight is positive when its concept grows toward + e i +e_{i} . We set α \alpha to leave a handful of concepts: 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} for the CLIP dictionary, 7 × 10 − 5 7\times 10^{-5} for the ImageNet-class dictionary, and 10 − 3 10^{-3} for the protein geometry dictionary ( 10 − 5 10^{-5} in the raw space of Appendix G ). Correlated concepts can exchange weight in such a fit. A weight therefore need not match the alignment of its concept direction alone with e i e_{i} , and we name a direction by its dominant concepts rather than by every surviving weight.

sections.heading: Images.
sections.text: We generate the sets with SD1.5 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) using the DDIM sampler ( Song et al., 2020 ) at classifier-free guidance scale 7.5 7.5 and 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution, at 15 , 20 , … , 50 15,20,\dots,50 steps, with one image per reference caption. The COCO reference is the 30,000 30{,}000 captioned images of the 2014 validation split. The Inception features are the 2048 2048 -dimensional pool features of clean-fid ( Parmar et al., 2022 ) . The CLIP dictionary uses CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336 336 pixels ( Radford et al., 2021 ) . It embeds each pole of a concept as the mean CLIP text embedding of its prompt set. The two groups are the top and bottom 10 % 10\% of reference images by the cosine similarity of their CLIP image embedding to the difference of the two pole embeddings. The 24 24 concepts are composition simplicity, number of objects, crowd density, people, indoor/outdoor, nature versus urban, animals, food, vehicles, furniture, electronics, sports equipment, close-up versus wide shot, colorfulness, warm versus cool tone, brightness, water and sky, text and signs, staged versus candid, centered composition, depth of field, weather, daytime, and portrait versus scene. The ImageNet-class dictionary is the 1008 1008 unit-normalized rows of the final Inception layer, which maps the pool features to the class logits. The DINOv2 check uses the ViT-L/14 model ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) with the same dictionary and penalty.

sections.heading: Video.
sections.text: The reference is 2048 2048 UCF-101 clips of 16 16 frames, one window per source video, at the 128 × 128 128\times 128 resolution both embeddings read ( Ge et al., 2024 ) . These 2048 2048 clips keep the covariance nondegenerate in the 1408 1408 dimensions of VideoMAE-v2. The distortions are the elastic transformation and motion blur of ImageNet-C at its five severities. We apply them at 128 128 pixels with the suite’s pixel constants, which are set for larger images, so they are harsher relative to the frame than in ImageNet-C. FVD uses the 400 400 -dimensional logits of the Kinetics-400 I3D classifier. The VideoMAE-v2 features are the 1408 1408 -dimensional outputs of its ViT-g model fine-tuned on Something-Something-v2, following Ge et al. (2024) . The bands for the flicker set at one severity average the displacements of the other four severities before taking eigenvectors. The bands for the generator average all five severities. ModelScope generates 2048 2048 clips of 16 16 frames from the UCF-101 class names with its default DPM-Solver scheduler at 25 25 steps, cropped like the reference.

sections.heading: Proteins.
sections.text: La-Proteina generates unconditional backbones from its released checkpoint. Each setting has 467 467 structures, the size of the Protein FID test set, which its default sampler spreads evenly over lengths of 100 100 , 200 200 , 300 300 , 400 400 , and 500 500 residues. The embeddings are ESM3 structure-token embeddings, mean-pooled to 1536 1536 dimensions with the sequence masked. The reference is the released embeddings of 4943 4943 curated PDB structures of Faltings et al. (2025) , each a FoldSeek cluster representative. The PCA to 32 32 dimensions is fit jointly on the reference and generated embeddings, as in Protein FID, and we recompute the optimal transport in this space. The concept dictionary is built from the 31,885 31{,}885 domains of the CATH S40 non-redundant set ( Sillitoe et al., 2021 ) . These domains are embedded the same way and projected onto the same PCA basis. The alpha-versus-beta direction runs from the mainly-alpha class to the mainly-beta class, and each geometric property is split at its terciles. The ten geometric properties are chain length, radius of gyration, globularity (the radius of gyration over the cube root of the length), the helix, strand, and coil fractions, the number of secondary-structure segments per residue, relative contact order, clashes per residue, and backbone-bond deviation, the standard deviation of consecutive alpha-carbon spacings.

sections.heading: Appendix E Sign reversal across references
sections.text: Section 4.1.2 decomposes the step-driven FID change on COCO into a rise over the head and a fall over the tail, where the rise outweighs the fall and FID rises with steps. The sign of this change is known to differ by reference ( Lee and Pak, 2026 ) , so we repeat the COCO sweep on six references and ask what sets the sign. The references are COCO30K, Flickr30K ( Young et al., 2014 ) , ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) , MJHQ30K ( Li et al., 2024 ) , CelebA-HQ ( Karras et al., 2017 ) , and FFHQ512 ( Karras et al., 2019 ) , spanning caption and object sets (COCO, Flickr, ImageNet), an aesthetic set (MJHQ), and two curated face sets. Each reference is compared with SD1.5 generations from its own captions, so the six comparisons differ in the generated set as well as in the reference. We compute each reference’s own eigenbasis of M M at 50 50 steps and hold it fixed throughout its sweep, as on COCO. The cumulative slope s 1 : i s_{1:i} of Section 4.1.2 ends at 1 on every reference, so it cannot compare the total change across references. We instead regress each FD ⁡ ( e i ) \mathrm{FD}(e_{i}) against the step count, and the cumulative sum β 1 : i = ∑ j ≤ i β j \beta_{1:i}=\sum_{j\leq i}\beta_{j} of the resulting slopes β i \beta_{i} ends at the total slope β FD \beta_{\mathrm{FD}} of FID against steps (Figure 4 ). Here β i \beta_{i} is the slope of the directional FD FD ⁡ ( e i ) \mathrm{FD}(e_{i}) against the step count, in each reference’s own fixed 50 50 -step basis. The curves of COCO, Flickr, ImageNet, and MJHQ rise over the head before falling over the tail, while the face curves descend throughout. Each endpoint is the total slope β FD \beta_{\mathrm{FD}} , which is positive for COCO, Flickr, and ImageNet, negative for the faces, and near zero for MJHQ. Rise and fall across references. The cumulative curves separate two effects that every reference shares in kind but not in size. The first is the head, led by e 1 e_{1} , along which the generated mean drifts as steps increase. The second is the tail, where directional FD falls with steps on every reference. The drift along e 1 e_{1} runs away from the reference on COCO, Flickr, ImageNet, and MJHQ, so their curves rise over the head before falling over the tail. The drift runs toward the reference on the two face references, so their curves fall throughout, with the decrease spread across the spectrum. The tail fall is of comparable size on every reference, so the head decides whether FID reverses. FID rises when the head rise outweighs the tail fall, falls when the drift runs toward the reference and the head falls too, and stays nearly flat when the two cancel. The change in the generated mean across the sweep, μ g ​ ( 50 ) − μ g ​ ( 15 ) \mu_{g}(50)-\mu_{g}(15) , aligns across all six comparisons (pairwise cosine 0.52 0.52 to 0.88 0.88 ), although their captions differ. Raising the step count thus moves the generated mean in a similar direction whatever the reference. Each reference’s FID, however, is carried by its own head, so the same drift contributes differently to each FID. The generated mean moves away from the reference along e 1 e_{1} on COCO, Flickr, and ImageNet, where the head rise exceeds the tail fall and FID worsens. The mean moves toward the reference along e 1 e_{1} on CelebA-HQ and FFHQ, and directional FD also decreases broadly across their spectra, so FID improves. MJHQ is the cancellation case: its discrepancy along e 1 e_{1} grows like that of the caption and object references, but the tail fall offsets it and leaves the total FID nearly unchanged. Finding. Adding steps drives the generated mean in a similar direction in every comparison. Each reference’s FID, however, is carried by its own head, so the reference decides whether FID reverses. The caption and object references (COCO, Flickr, ImageNet) worsen, the face references improve, and MJHQ cancels.

A Directional Decomposition Yunghee Lee Affiliation: Agency for Defense Development, South Korea Jaeyeon Kim Affiliation: Harvard University Abstract The Fréchet distance is a de facto standard for evaluating generative models across domains, appearing as FID for images and FVD for videos. It summarizes the discrepancy between generated and reference distributions in a single scalar, with lower values typically interpreted as better generation quality. However, this scalar view can obscure what drives the comparison. For example, in COCO dataset, increasing the number of diffusion sampling steps improves ImageReward scores yet worsens (increases) FID. Motivated by this mismatch, we seek to make the Fréchet distance more interpretable by uncovering where the discrepancy lies. To this end, we introduce directional Fréchet distance , the expected squared projection of the optimal transport displacement onto a given direction. Across our image, video, and protein case studies, we find that a small number of interpretable directions account for much of the distance. We use these directions to explain the FID increase in terms of semantic concepts represented by CLIP embeddings, quantify FVD’s bias toward per-frame appearance, and revisit the interpretation of Protein FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/yhlee-add/directional-fd . 1 Introduction Fréchet distance ( Dowson and Landau, 1982 ) underlies de facto evaluation metrics for generative models in continuous domains: Fréchet Inception distance (FID) for images ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , Fréchet video distance (FVD) for videos ( Unterthiner et al., 2018 ) , and Fréchet audio distance (FAD) for audio ( Kilgour et al., 2018 ) . A lower distance is read as a better generator, so the metric does not merely report progress but also defines it , steering architecture, sampling, and hyperparameter choices ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) . This influential signal, however, remains a scalar summary of a comparison between two high-dimensional feature distributions. This blind spot surfaces in recurring contradictions. For images, tuning a diffusion sampler configuration to minimize FID can drive per-sample quality to its worst ( Lee et al., 2026 ) ; stronger image distortions can even improve (lower) the metric ( Jayasumana et al., 2024 ) ; additional sampling steps can produce visibly sharper images ( Choi et al., 2025 ) , yet worsen FID on the COCO dataset ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . For videos, FVD favors per-frame appearance over motion, so a flickering clip can still score well ( Ge et al., 2024 ) . Prior work has sought to address these issues by refining Fréchet metrics or introducing scalar alternatives , such as changing the embedding ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2022 ) , adopting a kernel two-sample statistic ( Bińkowski et al., 2018 ; Jayasumana et al., 2024 ) , or reducing estimator bias ( Chong and Forsyth, 2020 ) . These changes can mitigate specific failures, but the resulting metrics still do not reveal where in feature space the distributions differ or what the discrepancy means. Contribution. In this work, we take a complementary approach: making existing Fréchet metrics interpretable. We introduce directional Fréchet distance , which measures the contribution of a fixed feature direction to the Fréchet distance. These directional distances sum to the Fréchet distance over any orthonormal basis, and the top eigenvectors of the displacement second-moment matrix inform where the discrepancy concentrates. We further affix these directions to interpretable concepts using CLIP concept bridges ( Kim et al., 2018 ; Bhalla et al., 2024 ) for images and structural-property concept directions for proteins. This gives semantic meaning to directional distances : a larger distance along a direction associated with a concept, e.g., composition simplicity or brightness, indicates that the metric attributes more of the discrepancy between generated and reference samples to that concept. With this lens, we revisit three established Fréchet metrics—FID, FVD, and Protein FID—to explain what drives previously reported discrepancies: • Images: In some reference datasets such as COCO, additional sampling steps can increase ImageReward but also increase FID ( Lee and Pak, 2026 ) . We find that two-thirds of this increase lies along a single direction in the feature space associated with composition simplicity. • Videos: In the controlled distortions of Ge et al. (2024) , I3D-based FVD responds weakly to added flicker. We find that the flicker band carries less of the distance than the appearance band with I3D features, but more with VideoMAE-v2 features. • Proteins: Protein FID was introduced to detect collapse onto a narrow range of easily foldable structures ( Faltings et al., 2025 ) , and its observed gap was partly attributed to missing beta sheets. We find that a single direction associated with structural regularity accounts for most of the gap, while the alpha-versus-beta direction accounts for little. 2 Preliminaries In Section 2.1 , we review the Fréchet distance and the family of metrics built from it. In Section 2.2 , we revisit prior observations across images and videos whose apparent contradictions stem from reading this single number as a measure of per-sample quality. 2.1 The Fréchet distance and its instances Fréchet distance is widely used to evaluate generative models by comparing Gaussian approximations to generated and reference distributions in a fixed feature space. A prominent example is Fréchet Inception distance (FID) ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , which uses InceptionV3 ( Szegedy et al., 2016 ) features. The Fréchet distance is the squared 2-Wasserstein distance between the fitted Gaussians, which admits the closed form FD = ‖ μ r − μ g ‖ 2 + Tr ⁡ ( Σ r + Σ g − 2 ​ ( Σ r 1 / 2 ​ Σ g ​ Σ r 1 / 2 ) 1 / 2 ) , \mathrm{FD}=\|\mu_{r}-\mu_{g}\|^{2}+\Tr\left(\Sigma_{r}+\Sigma_{g}-2\left(\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}\Sigma_{g}\Sigma_{r}^{1/2}\right)^{1/2}\right), (1) where ( μ r , Σ r ) (\mu_{r},\Sigma_{r}) and ( μ g , Σ g ) (\mu_{g},\Sigma_{g}) are the mean and covariance of the reference and generated feature distributions. The same Fréchet distance can also be computed over other embeddings such as CLIP ViT-L/14 ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) . The same recipe extends the metric across domains: Video is evaluated with FVD ( Unterthiner et al., 2018 ) , the Fréchet distance over I3D embeddings ( Carreira and Zisserman, 2017 ) , and protein structure generation has recently adopted Protein FID ( Faltings et al., 2025 ) over ESM3 structure-token embeddings ( Hayes et al., 2025 ) . Across all of these, a full comparison between two distributions is reduced to a single number, which reports that they differ but not where . 2.2 Contradictory observations A lower Fréchet distance is commonly interpreted as a higher-quality generator. This interpretation suggests that improvements in per-sample quality should be accompanied by a decrease in distance. In this section, we present two prior observations that challenge this. To begin with, we first formally define the per-sample quality : for a chosen sample-level scoring function q q , we denote the quality of generator G G to be 𝔼 x ∼ G ​ [ q ​ ( x ) ] \mathbb{E}_{x\sim G}[q(x)] . Examples of such scoring functions include CLIP score ( Hessel et al., 2021 ) , ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , and the numerical accuracy of each sample. Raising the classifier-free guidance scale ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) makes each sample match the prompt better and improves ImageReward, yet FID on the COCO reference dataset ( Lin et al., 2014 ) worsens monotonically ( Lee et al., 2026 , Table 8) . We call this contradictory phenomenon sign reversal : a change that raises per-sample quality raises the Fréchet distance instead of lowering it. Sign reversal makes FID an unreliable gate on generation quality. A sampling algorithm ( Lu et al., 2025 ) or an inference accelerator ( Kim et al., 2025 ) is accepted once it matches or lowers FID, read as evidence that quality is preserved. Under sign reversal, that inference is invalid, since the same low FID is equally consistent with per-sample quality having dropped, and the verdict on the method no longer follows. Videos. FVD computes the Fréchet distance in the feature space of I3D ( Carreira and Zisserman, 2017 ) , a video model pretrained for action recognition. In practice, however, FVD favors per-frame appearance over motion ( Ge et al., 2024 ) : a clip whose individual frames are realistic can still score well when it flickers. To address this, Ge et al. (2024) propose replacing I3D features with self-supervised video embeddings such as VideoMAE-v2 ( Wang et al., 2023b ) , improving sensitivity to motion while retaining the same Fréchet distance computation. 3 Directional Fréchet distance The contradictory observations of Section 2.2 highlight a limitation of interpreting Fréchet distance (FD) as a measure of per-sample quality: FD aggregates discrepancies across feature directions into a single value, obscuring which of them drive it. The backbone is considered designable if the predicted structure matches it within a self-consistency RMSD (scRMSD) of 2 2 Å ( Trippe et al., 2022 ; Watson et al., 2023 ) . High designability, however, can be achieved by generating mostly alpha-helical backbones: alpha helices rely largely on local hydrogen bonds, whereas beta sheets require long-range coordination. Optimizing for designability can therefore favor a narrow range of easily foldable, helix-rich structures while losing beta sheets from the generated distribution. To detect such collapse, Faltings et al. (2025) introduce Protein FID, the Fréchet distance between generated and reference structures embedded with the ESM3 structure encoder ( Hayes et al., 2025 ) . They validate it through its monotone response to structural perturbations and its recovery of the FoldSeek and CATH hierarchies. The authors partly attribute the Protein FID gap to missing beta sheets, based on a sample-level influence analysis that identifies large alpha-helical bundles as major contributors. We use directional FD to examine which structural directions drive the gap: the alpha-versus-beta contrast accounts for only a small share, whereas a single direction associated with structural regularity accounts for the largest share. Reference and embedding. Protein FID mean-pools the per-residue ESM3 embeddings to 1536 1536 dimensions. It then applies a PCA to 32 32 dimensions, fit jointly over the reference and generated embeddings, because the raw covariances are nearly degenerate ( Faltings et al., 2025 ) . We analyze this 32 32 -dimensional space and recompute the optimal transport in it. The reference is the released embeddings of curated PDB structures. The raw space gives the same picture (Appendix G ). Generations and concept directions. The alpha-versus-beta direction carries only 5.5 % 5.5\% , so Protein FID charges over-regularity far more than the missing beta sheets. 5 Conclusion In this work, we introduced directional Fréchet distance, decomposing Fréchet distance along an orthonormal basis of feature directions. Across images, videos, and proteins, this viewpoint facilitates explaining the sign reversal of FID and the content bias of FVD, and revisits a prior interpretation of Protein FID. Outlook. More broadly, we hope this work prompts a rethinking of what scalar evaluation can and cannot tell us. A scalar score is useful per se –it makes models easy to compare, spurring competition and progress in generative modeling. Nevertheless, it does not reveal which aspects of a distribution a model fails to capture. Directional FD opens the door to more interpretable evaluation of generative models.
